content.overview: Section 109 lets the chairman order a poll, and requires a poll on a valid demand. For a company with share capital the demand is by members with at least one-tenth of the voting power, or holding shares on which at least five lakh rupees has been paid up. A poll on the chairman or an adjournment is taken forthwith. Any other poll is taken as the chairman directs, not later than forty-eight hours.
content.glance: A poll may be ordered by the chair or demanded by the members specified in the section, and is taken as the chair directs.
content.study:
## Statutory rule
Section 109(1) lets the chairman order a poll on his own motion, and requires him to order a poll on a demand by the members the section names. For a company having a share capital, the demand is by members present in person or by proxy, where allowed, having not less than one-tenth of the total voting power, or holding shares on which an aggregate sum of not less than five lakh rupees, or such higher amount as may be prescribed, has been paid up. For any other company, the demand is by members having not less than one-tenth of the total voting power.

Section 109(2) lets the persons who demanded the poll withdraw the demand.

Section 109(3) and (4) require a poll on the election of the chairman or on an adjournment to be taken forthwith. A poll on any other question is taken at the time the chairman directs, not later than forty-eight hours from the demand.

Section 109(5) and (6) let the chairman regulate the manner of the poll. The result of the poll is the decision of the meeting on that resolution.

## Answer structure
State who demanded the poll and whether the threshold is met. Then state whether it is taken forthwith or within forty-eight hours. Not a verified closure.

sections.body: The demand threshold is members present or by proxy having not less than one-tenth of the total voting power, or holding shares on which an aggregate sum of not less than five lakh rupees has been paid up. cases.name: Salomon v. A. Salomon & Co. Ltd.
cases.facts: A properly incorporated company was challenged as indistinct from its controlling shareholder.
cases.issue: What is the legal effect of incorporation?
cases.ratioDecidendi: A registered company is a legal person separate from its members, even when control and ownership are concentrated.
cases.holding: The company's separate personality was affirmed.
cases.relevance: Use for Companies Act s. 9 and corporate personality.

cases.name: Foss v. Harbottle
cases.facts: Shareholders sought relief for alleged wrongs to the company.
cases.issue: Who may sue for a wrong done to the company and when may exceptions apply?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The company is the proper plaintiff for corporate wrongs, subject to recognised exceptions such as fraud on the minority and ultra vires acts.
cases.holding: The proper-plaintiff and majority-rule principles were established.
cases.relevance: Use with oppression, mismanagement and class-action analysis.

cases.name: Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court examined share issue powers and alleged oppression.
cases.issue: When does a corporate action become oppressive or invalid?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examines purpose, fairness, statutory power and resulting prejudice rather than treating every irregularity as oppression.
cases.holding: The corporate action was assessed under the statutory and equitable framework.
cases.relevance: Use for share allotment and oppression claims.

cases.name: Miheer H. Mafatlal v. Mafatlal Industries Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court reviewed a scheme of arrangement sanctioned by the company court.
cases.issue: What is the court's role in sanctioning a corporate scheme?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The court must ensure statutory compliance, class fairness, informed approval and absence of illegality, but does not substitute its commercial judgment for the company's decision.
cases.holding: The principles governing scheme sanction were stated.
cases.relevance: Use for corporate arrangements and tribunal scrutiny.

enhancement.detailedExplanation: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 109 (Demand for poll). A poll may be ordered by the chair or demanded by the members specified in the section, and is taken as the chair directs. The section applies only to the persons, companies, and transactions it names. A filing, approval, or penalty arises only where the section or a rule under it says so. It does not create a power that is reserved to another section or to the Tribunal. Not a verified closure.
